I see how some people can watch flashy robot demos on the timeline and think with a shiver that the robot apocalypse is around the corner, but reality check: There is no robot in the world that can change the batteries in a jack-o-lantern. If you have a robot friendly door handle it might be able to walk outside, pick it up, and carry it back inside. The robot could open the drawer with your batteries in it, but then things get tough. Opening the package of AA batteries? Extracting a precision screwdriver from its case? Unscrewing four tiny screws that require a hard press and twist? Popping batteries out of the case? Yes, you could build and train a specialist robot to do that today, but there is a very long way to go to replace the full range of human capabilities. Near term doomer scenarios should stop at “secretly controlling humanity” instead of “wiping humanity out” 😀

RAG is so back! Another paper showing that plain RAG keeps winning the agent memory comparison. They show that many dedicated memory systems score below naive retrieval over the raw history on LongMemEval, PersonaMem, and MINT-Eval, while costing much more. They split a memory system's value into two parts. Memory benefit counts questions it answers that RAG misses. Memory tax counts questions RAG answers that the memory system gets wrong. Why does the tax appear? Building memory rewrites the history. Some facts get dropped or distorted during extraction, and some survive but become harder to retrieve. Memory systems also vary more than RAG when you change the backbone model. A simple fix helped. Retrieving from the raw history alongside memory and reranking both together reduced the tax. The practical takeaway here is that before adding a memory layer to your agent, compare it with plain retrieval over the transcript on your own data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34073 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/memory-tax-dissecting-the-net-value-of-agent-memory-2610.34073

"We saw a glimpse of the future of swarm coding." Agent swarms will fundamentally change how we build software. @axiommathai used a swarm of agents to formally verify the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the largest proof in math history. That is roughly 15,000 pages by over 100 mathematicians, now about 50 million lines of Lean, verified in 24 days. The agents claimed tasks, wrote proofs, reviewed each other, and merged their own work through GitHub. Along the way, they fixed hundreds of major errata in the published proof. The largest math proof in human history is now computer-verified. Today, Axiom announces a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the "periodic table of symmetry." About 15,000 pages, built by over 100 mathematicians across generations.
